scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: New EN/C2 independent Reading questions; unapproved teacher review draft.

tabs.title: Interpreting the Argument
tabs.description: Identify the implications of the author's claims.

tabs.title: Claims and Qualifications
tabs.description: Examine the structure and limits of reasoning.

tabs.title: Critical Application
tabs.description: Apply the argument to unfamiliar educational situations.

questions.q: Why might telling a struggling pupil to 'bounce back' amount to an evasion of responsibility?
choices: The exhortation can disregard the continuing conditions that made the setback damaging
It presumes that failure necessarily reveals a lack of personal resilience
It implies that assessment cannot capture genuine intellectual progress
The advice is generally effective only after a learner's difficulties have ended
questions.explanation: The opening criticises perseverance advice imposed irrespective of ongoing material constraints.

questions.q: What separates an exercise of agency from the endurance described in the second paragraph?
choices: Agency produces visibly higher grades, whereas endurance rarely does
Endurance is an irrational reaction to criticism in every circumstance
Agency involves adjusting a strategy where support makes meaningful progress plausible
Agency requires a pupil to disregard obstacles that are outside their control
questions.explanation: The text contrasts revising an ineffective method with repeatedly compensating for inadequate support.

questions.q: Which condition determines whether renewed effort can reasonably be expected to help?
choices: The pupil's willingness to display determination to others
The learner's circumstances provide a realistic chance of consequential change
The institution rewards endurance regardless of academic outcome
A pupil can repeat the same strategy with greater intensity
questions.explanation: The second paragraph asks whether the learner's environment offers a reasonable prospect of meaningful change.

questions.q: What does the metaphor of performance indicators 'colonising' education imply?
choices: Quantitative measures eventually become too unreliable to calculate
The activities being measured inevitably become less demanding
The institutional incentives surrounding measurement cease to matter
Measures start shaping which experiences count instead of merely describing them
questions.explanation: The metaphor suggests that progress indicators intrude upon activities they were designed to illuminate.

questions.q: Why does the writer concede that an indicator may be 'not necessarily false'?
choices: A narrowly accurate measure can still miss educationally important dimensions
Imprecise progress data is more useful than a judgement of intellectual maturity
The difference between exploration and repetition cannot be measured at all
The author's proposed alternatives would necessarily produce comparable statistics
questions.explanation: The problem is the indicator's restricted scope, not necessarily factual inaccuracy.

questions.q: What does the rejection of a return to 'fixed talent' accomplish in the argument?
choices: It denies the existence of meaningful differences in learners' resources
It prevents the critique of resilience from being mistaken for a denial of agency
It makes the author's critique dependent on the rejection of all assessment
It suggests that effort has no role in learning without institutional support
questions.explanation: The author explicitly resists the false alternative between unqualified perseverance and powerlessness.

questions.q: A school chiefly rewards rapid rises in scores, overlooking pupils who explore difficult ideas. What is the problem?
choices: The assessment assumes that unfamiliar ideas are always harder than familiar questions
The school has insufficiently differentiated the grading scale between subjects
It risks treating a restricted metric as a complete account of educational progress
The pupils with lower gains must be practising less effectively than their peers
questions.explanation: The example in paragraph three warns that score gains answer only a narrower question.

questions.q: A student abandons an ill-chosen goal after careful reflection. What would this reveal in the author's framework?
choices: Potentially mature judgement about the ends that perseverance ought to serve
A loss of resilience that educational institutions should try to correct
An inability to tolerate uncertainty despite sufficient external support
Evidence that the original goal was necessarily impossible to attain
questions.explanation: The third and fourth paragraphs allow reconsidering a goal rather than persisting ritualistically.

questions.q: What is the institutional risk of repeatedly praising pupils for overcoming the same preventable obstacle?
choices: Pupils will cease to believe that effort can improve results
Praise may deflect attention from the school's responsibility for persistent conditions
The institution may overestimate the reliability of its assessment indicators
Teachers will become unable to distinguish agency from intellectual curiosity
questions.explanation: Celebrating visible endurance can spare an institution from asking why the obstacle remains.

questions.q: Which statement most faithfully preserves the author's proposed educational balance?
choices: All evaluation ought to give way to freely chosen learning experiences
Students should always determine institutional priorities for assessment
Structural constraints ought to excuse pupils from reconsidering their goals
Institutions should enable persistence while leaving learners free to question its purpose
questions.explanation: The conclusion gives learners both means to continue and freedom to reconsider worthwhile goals.
